title: 4 Million Sweat Glands: Why Do Some People Sweat More?
description:
Why do some people sweat so much more than others? This animated explainer shows how your 2 to 4 million sweat glands switch on, why body size, genes and fitness change how much you sweat, and why sweating a lot often means you're fitter.

Sources:
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/eccrine-glands
https://www.livescience.com/8725-women-sweat-effectively-men.html
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710196

Animated in the Flat-Vector Science style.

topic: Why do some people sweat so much more than others?
script:
You have up to four million sweat glands.
So why do some people drip,
while others barely look damp?
Picture two people, same hot room, same workout.
One is soaked. The other is fine.
It's not about being healthy or unhealthy.
It comes down to your body's cooling system,
and how hard it's been trained.
Let's start with the hardware.
Your skin is packed with two to four million sweat glands.
Each one is a tiny coiled tube,
buried in your skin like a curly straw.
They cover almost your whole body,
with the most on your palms, the soles of your feet,
and your forehead.
Now here's how they switch on.
Deep in your brain sits a thermostat called the hypothalamus.
When your core gets even slightly too warm,
it fires a signal down your nerves.
The glands squeeze out salty water onto your skin.
And then comes the clever part.
Sweat doesn't cool you by being wet.
It cools you by disappearing.
When it evaporates, it carries heat away with it.
That's why a humid day feels so awful.
The air is already full of water,
so your sweat just sits there and drips.
And fresh sweat barely smells at all.
The smell comes from bacteria
munching on sweat from your armpit glands.
So why does one person drip while another stays dry?
First, size.
A bigger body makes more heat when it moves,
so it needs more sweat to dump it.
Second, your genes.
Some people simply have more active glands,
or glands that pump harder.
Third, men and women tend to differ.
In a study in Japan,
fit men started sweating fastest of everyone,
and inactive women sweated the least.
But here's the twist most people get backwards.
Sweating a lot usually means you're fitter, not less fit.
A trained body is like an upgraded air conditioner.
It turns on sooner,
before you even feel hot,
and it pumps out more sweat once it gets going.
Heat training does the same thing.
Spend around one to two weeks exercising in the heat,
and your body starts sweating earlier,
pours out more,
and holds on to more of its salt.
Now let's talk numbers.
Sitting still on a cool day,
you lose a little sweat without ever noticing.
But during hard exercise in the heat,
an adult can sweat more than a litre an hour.
Some athletes lose two litres or more.
That's a big bottle of water,
leaving your body through your skin.
And every drop that evaporates
pulls a surprising amount of heat out with it.
So why does all this matter?
Because sweating is one of humanity's superpowers.
Most furry animals cool down by panting.
We cool our whole body surface at once,
which is part of why humans are so good
at long, slow runs in the heat.
So if you're the one dripping at the gym,
don't be embarrassed.
Your cooling system might just be top of the line.
Just remember to drink water and replace what you lose.
Next time, why do you have two nostrils,
and why is one of them always more blocked?
key_facts: Humans have about 2-4 million eccrine sweat glands (Cleveland Clinic)
The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat and triggers sweating
Sweat cools by evaporating; humid air slows evaporation
Fresh sweat is nearly odourless; smell comes from bacteria breaking down apocrine (armpit) sweat
Bigger bodies make more heat and sweat more
2010 Osaka International University study: fit men sweated most readily, inactive women least (LiveScience)
Fit people start sweating at a lower core temperature and can sweat more (LiveScience, Precision Hydration)
Heat acclimation over roughly 1-2 weeks: earlier onset, higher sweat rate, more salt conserved
Hard exercise in heat: over 1 L/hour, some athletes 2 L+ (PMC3710196)
